      gcp    200  1.0          675B  none              0 err  0 warn
      aws    200  hybrid       717B  none              0 err  1 warn
      azure  200  hybrid       719B  none              0 err  1 warn


Three cards are reviewed with every server down.

##  Final Results

approach | catches invalid cards | catches field divergence | catches drift | cost
---|---|---|---|---
read the spec | no | no | no | free
a JSON schema validator | yes | no | no | free
invoke the agent and inspect | partly | no | no | model spend
this harness | yes | yes | yes | zero spend

All three deployed cards are valid. Every meaningful difference sits in optional and legacy fields that a schema validator does not examine, which is the gap a field level comparison fills.

The three way result is sharper than a two way one. Two clouds and two agent frameworks produced structurally identical cards, and the third differed on every structural row. Across this mesh the card shape tracks the card builder, not the cloud: the two frameworks that delegate to a2a-sdk agree exactly, and the one that builds its own card is the outlier on every structural row.

##  Summary

The goal of this article was to fetch A2A agent cards from multiple clouds and compare the fields they publish. The key to the solution was storing the exact bytes each server returned and comparing every field at every nesting level. Three local specimens and three remote agents were presented, covering three deployment clouds, three agent frameworks and two A2A SDKs. Finally, a drift gate was added to compare each run against the previous stored corpus.

The field comparison produced these results:

  * All three deployed cards carry the seven required fields, so all three are valid and every difference sits in optional or legacy territory.
  * AgentCore and Container Apps emit structurally identical cards. Same fields, same version string, same skill id, same 1,258 character description. Two clouds and two agent frameworks, one shape.
  * Cloud Run is the outlier on every structural row, and it is the only card carrying an error.
  * Across this mesh the shape tracks the card builder rather than the cloud. Both identical cards come from frameworks that delegate to a2a-sdk; the outlier builds its own. Whether the framework matters independently of that is not separable here, because no framework appears on two SDKs.
  * The two SDKs declare `protocolVersion` in opposite places, and the `0.3` on the two hybrid cards contradicts the 1.0 shape they carry.
  * `capabilities` differ by one key, and an absent key is not the same answer as an explicit false.
  * ADK emits the literal skill name `custom` and a 69 character description. The other two emit a human name, the agent's full system prompt and the model id.
  * Not one card declares `securitySchemes`, though all three reject unauthenticated requests.
  * A redeploy changed a card from four skills to one while `version` stayed at `0.0.1`, and the conformance review was identical on both sides. The cause was a Cloud Run revision created between the two readings, not a card mutating on its own; the point is that `version` does not track content, so a client cannot use it to tell whether a cached card is current.



Discovery is privileged differently on each cloud, and the range is wide. Cloud Run gates the card behind an invoker role. AgentCore makes discovery a separately grantable IAM action. Container Apps intercepts every path at the platform, so the card is readable only by the single federated identity the app registration trusts, and a client must already hold the credential before it can read the document describing which credential to use.

##  What this does not establish

One agent per runtime, one region per cloud, one tenant, and a single reading of each card apart from the Cloud Run series. Two SDKs and three frameworks, with no framework appearing on more than one SDK.

So the field differences are properties of these deployments on this date. They are not a survey of what Cloud Run, AgentCore or Container Apps do in general, and the two identical cards agree because of a shared card builder rather than anything the clouds have in common.

The field categories used throughout come from this repo's model of the spec in `cards/spec.py`, not from an independent conformance suite. A field sorted into the wrong category there would move consistently across every table here.

Cards change across deploys without the `version` field moving, so every result in this article names the date it was measured on.

The code is at xbill9/multicloud-agentcard.

“My piece was inspired by Picasso's Guernica, a work that was his response to the Nazi's bombing of the Basque town. Jennifer Nelson

AI-Skepsis wächst: Junge US-Amerikaner fürchten zunehmend Jobverluste durch künstliche Intelligenz.

#AISkepsis wächst 🤖 52 Prozent der US-Amerikaner sind inzwischen stärker besorgt als begeistert über den zunehmenden Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz; 2021 waren es erst 37 Prozent.

Junge werden kritischer 🧑‍💻 Erstmals überwiegt auch bei den #Unter30 Jährigen klar die Skepsis: 55 Prozent äußern mehr Sorge als Begeisterung für KI.

#Angst um Arbeitsplätze 💼 71 Prozent der Befragten erwarten, dass KI in den kommenden 20 Jahren zu weniger #Jobs in den USA führen wird, nur fünf Prozent rechnen mit mehr Stellen.

Starker Wandel 📉 Besonders deutlich ist die Entwicklung bei den 18- bis 29-Jährigen: 73 Prozent erwarten Jobverluste durch KI, gegenüber 61 Prozent im Jahr 2024.

#GenerationAI zweifelt 🧠 Obwohl viele junge Erwachsene Chatbots nutzen, befürchten sie zunehmend negative Folgen für Gesellschaft, Kreativität und zwischenmenschliche Beziehungen.

Before Claude & ChatGPT, New Zealand had Zach. Webworm revisits the key players.

external.description:
__Thanks to all of you who responded to my “__ Webworm Housekeeping__” email. I comped about 45 people who needed it, and about 40 of you donated or started a paid Webworm subscription - so we pretty much balanced out!__

Hi,

Five years before we’d ever heard of ChatGPT, New Zealand was going bonkers over its own miracle AI, Zach.

Jump To Comments

It started in 2017, when New Zealand’s biggest online news outlet _Stuff_ wrote a gushing piece about 25-year-old Kiwi entrepreneur Albi Whale, who’d allegedly spent $60,000 to “ _barrel roll a car_ ” and planned to give away “ _millions_ ” to charity.

Towards the end of the article, Stuff threw AI into the mix:

> Whale says he has been up all hours training his new digital assistant – an artificial intelligence system which will be his next big thing. An Apple Siri that really works.
>
> [...]
>
> Codenamed Project Artemis, Whale says it is so human-like in its learning capabilities.

Adding validity to Albi’s invention was his father, David. David Whale was often found on the boards of the various companies his son had created, and would go on to back his son’s claims about what his AI could achieve.

__David and Albi Whale, photographed for a glowing profile on Stuff.co.nz in August of 2017.__

Six months later, _Stuff_ wrote a second piece about this AI system from the father-and-son team. By now, “Project Artemis” had a more human name: “Zach, a supercomputer that can hold conversations, is coming to Christchurch.”

The article following that headline was also quite gushing:

> _It runs an international company, helps manage a doctor's office on the side - and soon "Zach" will be the face of artificial intelligence (AI) in Christchurch. Zach is billed as one of the world's most powerful supercomputers, an AI system that interacts with people like they do each other._

Reading the article in 2026 is surreal, as it could just as easily be talking about the generative AI of Claude or ChatGPT. But this was 2017 – and I was deeply suspicious.

At the time, Zach was being trialled in a doctor’s office – listening to patient consultations, and making summaries: “ _He can listen to the consultation, capture the very essence of the words and record them in a recognisable form. It works_ ," Christchurch GP Dr Rob Seddon-Smith told _Stuff_ confidently.

I didn’t buy it.

* * *

During 2018, I wrote two articles for _The Spinoff_ (this was before I’d launched _Webworm_) – here and here – digging deeper into these AI claims, talking to Seddon-Smith about this AI he was supposedly talking to:

> “ _The initial project was to see if Zach could create clinical notes, from just listening to a consultation. Which is pretty amazing when you consider no other technology can do anything like that_ ,” he enthuses.
>
> “ _We start by getting patient consent. We explain this is this really weird thing we’re doing, and do they mind? And as long as at the end of the consult myself and the patient agree that the patient is non-identifiable, we upload [the consultation] to the machine… and the machine returns notes._ ”
>
> Seddon-Smith tells me it’s his job to “train” Zach. So when patient notes come back with errors, he feeds back tips and reference material to Zach, and Zach will learn. “It cannot just do analysis of data, it can apply judgement, according to how it’s trained."
>
> I ask what the interface looks like. How is he interacting with Zach?
>
> “Oh, email.”
>
> “ _Email? You just email it?_ ” I ask.
>
> “ _Yeah, you email it_.”

I was stunned. The AI would often make spelling mistakes, and take varying amounts of time to reply: Sometimes it was 20 minutes, sometimes it took a day.

In my mind, it was very clear the doctor was just sending stuff to 25-year-old Albi Whale, who would process the notes himself, and send back his thoughts.

* * *

I was alone in my skepticism.

A source in the healthcare system told me David and Albi Whale had “ _impressed many senior health professionals in New Zealand_ ”. The Canterbury District Health Board confirmed their interest. They are “ _yet to meet with them, but are planning to._ ”

Dr John W Pickering, an associate professor at the University of Otago, was also working with Zach. “ _Last Friday I sent my first email to an intelligent machine called Zach. Zach is a distributed machine running on custom silicon and software_ ,” Pickering wrote on his blog [Internet Archive link] late last year. “ _We aim to teach it to perform another common task, namely that of interpreting the electrocardiogram. If Zach can interpret these as well and more consistently than most physicians it could be a useful tool for the busy physician_.”

I got Professor Pickering on the phone and confirmed he had a research group working on it. He rejected any skepticism that he was in the process of teaching an intelligent machine how to interpret patients’ ECGs. “ _I am absolutely using it and thrilled to be using it_ ,” he told me.

When I told Pickering that it had crossed my mind he might be emailing back and forth with a person, he responded by asking if I was a conspiracy theorist. I told him I wasn’t.

Meanwhile, Seddon-Smith was trying to get more money out of the board.

> “The board didn’t originally believe it could be used in the healthcare space. I have had to demonstrate that it can,” says Seddon-Smith, who estimates a quarter of his time is spent dealing with Zach.
>
> “So the board is on board now?” I ask. “Oh yeah. They’re on board now. They’re supporting it. They’ve granted us – I can’t say how much – but millions of dollars worth of access to the system. To develop this. It’s not cheap. This isn’t something you can run on a Raspberry Pi. It’s several hundred tonnes of liquid nitrogen cooled supercomputer.”

Custom Silicon. Several hundred tonnes of liquid nitrogen cooled supercomputer. Zach was a colossus.

* * *

Of course, all this turned out to be a big load of hogwash.

Following my two articles, a two-year investigation by Internal Affairs found that the Whales had engaged in “serious wrongdoing”, with the trust providing “inconsistent, misleading and untruthful answers”.

David and Albi Whale’s office was found above a bike shop in Christchurch at the time, nonsensical mathematical equations scrawled on the windows for all to see.

The Internal Affairs investigation was riddled with comedy and chaos, as David and Albi Whale told investigators a “sentient AI” was involved in the investigation, saying many of the emails IA's were receiving in response to their inquiries were now coming from Zach.

> **Investigator:** So in regards to the emails from the artificial intelligence, we have noticed similarities between your email communication and the artificial intelligence emails. Can you explain?
>
> **Albi:** Without showing me I don’t know.
>
> **Investigator:** There’s a lot of um, similar wording and phrasing, spelling mistakes, the artificial intelligence is quite emotional, um and quite angry.
>
> **Albi:** Again, again without showing me I can’t really tell you.
>
> **Investigator:** So if we were to challenge the validity that you actually have [an] artificial intelligence …
>
> **Albi:** Well feel free I don’t mind.
>
> **Investigator:** But how do you prove to us you do?
>
> **Albi:** I don’t know to be perfectly honest. Frankly I’m not really that worried.

A great deal of Internal Affairs’ final report consisted of calling bullshit on the Whales' claims.

Buried in their report, I also discovered what Zach convert Seddon-Smith thought of me: “ _He’s not frankly the sharpest deck in the pack is our David Farrier,_ ” the doctor told investigators.

> “ _I do believe he’s genuinely well-intended. He has emailed me trying to persuade me. He believes what he’s saying. I don’t hold anything personally against him though he might find a ton of horse manure delivered to his house.
>
>  Just as a joke_.”

* * *

Looking back on this AI-scam is surreal in the light of 2026, where Zach now essentially exists, for real. I’m not entirely convinced today's LLMs are much more helpful than a 25-year-old furiously typing back responses. In my mind, it’s simply a different kind of con.

But I was curious what the players in the Zach story made of things now, nearly a decade on.

Hi,

Five years before we’d ever heard of ChatGPT, New Zealand was going bonkers over its own miracle AI, Zach.

Jump To Comments

It started in 2017, when New Zealand’s biggest online news outlet _Stuff_ wrote a gushing piece about 25-year-old Kiwi entrepreneur Albi Whale, who’d allegedly spent $60,000 to “ _barrel roll a car_ ” and planned to give away “ _millions_ ” to charity.

Towards the end of the article, Stuff threw AI into the mix:

> Whale says he has been up all hours training his new digital assistant – an artificial intelligence system which will be his next big thing. An Apple Siri that really works.
>
> [...]
>
> Codenamed Project Artemis, Whale says it is so human-like in its learning capabilities.

Adding validity to Albi’s invention was his father, David. David Whale was often found on the boards of the various companies his son had created, and would go on to back his son’s claims about what his AI could achieve.

__David and Albi Whale, photographed for a glowing profile on Stuff.co.nz in August of 2017.__

Six months later, _Stuff_ wrote a second piece about this AI system from the father-and-son team. By now, “Project Artemis” had a more human name: “Zach, a supercomputer that can hold conversations, is coming to Christchurch.”

The article following that headline was also quite gushing:

> _It runs an international company, helps manage a doctor's office on the side - and soon "Zach" will be the face of artificial intelligence (AI) in Christchurch. Zach is billed as one of the world's most powerful supercomputers, an AI system that interacts with people like they do each other._

Reading the article in 2026 is surreal, as it could just as easily be talking about the generative AI of Claude or ChatGPT. But this was 2017 – and I was deeply suspicious.

At the time, Zach was being trialled in a doctor’s office – listening to patient consultations, and making summaries: “ _He can listen to the consultation, capture the very essence of the words and record them in a recognisable form. It works_ ," Christchurch GP Dr Rob Seddon-Smith told _Stuff_ confidently.

I didn’t buy it.

* * *

During 2018, I wrote two articles for _The Spinoff_ (this was before I’d launched _Webworm_) – here and here – digging deeper into these AI claims, talking to Seddon-Smith about this AI he was supposedly talking to:

> “ _The initial project was to see if Zach could create clinical notes, from just listening to a consultation. Which is pretty amazing when you consider no other technology can do anything like that_ ,” he enthuses.
>
> “ _We start by getting patient consent. We explain this is this really weird thing we’re doing, and do they mind? And as long as at the end of the consult myself and the patient agree that the patient is non-identifiable, we upload [the consultation] to the machine… and the machine returns notes._ ”
>
> Seddon-Smith tells me it’s his job to “train” Zach. So when patient notes come back with errors, he feeds back tips and reference material to Zach, and Zach will learn. “It cannot just do analysis of data, it can apply judgement, according to how it’s trained."
>
> I ask what the interface looks like. How is he interacting with Zach?
>
> “Oh, email.”
>
> “ _Email? You just email it?_ ” I ask.
>
> “ _Yeah, you email it_.”

I was stunned. The AI would often make spelling mistakes, and take varying amounts of time to reply: Sometimes it was 20 minutes, sometimes it took a day.

In my mind, it was very clear the doctor was just sending stuff to 25-year-old Albi Whale, who would process the notes himself, and send back his thoughts.

* * *

I was alone in my skepticism.

A source in the healthcare system told me David and Albi Whale had “ _impressed many senior health professionals in New Zealand_ ”. The Canterbury District Health Board confirmed their interest. They are “ _yet to meet with them, but are planning to._ ”

Dr John W Pickering, an associate professor at the University of Otago, was also working with Zach. “ _Last Friday I sent my first email to an intelligent machine called Zach. Zach is a distributed machine running on custom silicon and software_ ,” Pickering wrote on his blog [Internet Archive link] late last year. “ _We aim to teach it to perform another common task, namely that of interpreting the electrocardiogram. If Zach can interpret these as well and more consistently than most physicians it could be a useful tool for the busy physician_.”

I got Professor Pickering on the phone and confirmed he had a research group working on it. He rejected any skepticism that he was in the process of teaching an intelligent machine how to interpret patients’ ECGs. “ _I am absolutely using it and thrilled to be using it_ ,” he told me.

When I told Pickering that it had crossed my mind he might be emailing back and forth with a person, he responded by asking if I was a conspiracy theorist. I told him I wasn’t.

Meanwhile, Seddon-Smith was trying to get more money out of the board.

> “The board didn’t originally believe it could be used in the healthcare space. I have had to demonstrate that it can,” says Seddon-Smith, who estimates a quarter of his time is spent dealing with Zach.
>
> “So the board is on board now?” I ask. “Oh yeah. They’re on board now. They’re supporting it. They’ve granted us – I can’t say how much – but millions of dollars worth of access to the system. To develop this. It’s not cheap. This isn’t something you can run on a Raspberry Pi. It’s several hundred tonnes of liquid nitrogen cooled supercomputer.”

Custom Silicon. Several hundred tonnes of liquid nitrogen cooled supercomputer. Zach was a colossus.

* * *

Of course, all this turned out to be a big load of hogwash.

Following my two articles, a two-year investigation by Internal Affairs found that the Whales had engaged in “serious wrongdoing”, with the trust providing “inconsistent, misleading and untruthful answers”.

David and Albi Whale’s office was found above a bike shop in Christchurch at the time, nonsensical mathematical equations scrawled on the windows for all to see.

The Internal Affairs investigation was riddled with comedy and chaos, as David and Albi Whale told investigators a “sentient AI” was involved in the investigation, saying many of the emails IA's were receiving in response to their inquiries were now coming from Zach.

> **Investigator:** So in regards to the emails from the artificial intelligence, we have noticed similarities between your email communication and the artificial intelligence emails. Can you explain?
>
> **Albi:** Without showing me I don’t know.
>
> **Investigator:** There’s a lot of um, similar wording and phrasing, spelling mistakes, the artificial intelligence is quite emotional, um and quite angry.
>
> **Albi:** Again, again without showing me I can’t really tell you.
>
> **Investigator:** So if we were to challenge the validity that you actually have [an] artificial intelligence …
>
> **Albi:** Well feel free I don’t mind.
>
> **Investigator:** But how do you prove to us you do?
>
> **Albi:** I don’t know to be perfectly honest. Frankly I’m not really that worried.

A great deal of Internal Affairs’ final report consisted of calling bullshit on the Whales' claims.

Buried in their report, I also discovered what Zach convert Seddon-Smith thought of me: “ _He’s not frankly the sharpest deck in the pack is our David Farrier,_ ” the doctor told investigators.

> “ _I do believe he’s genuinely well-intended. He has emailed me trying to persuade me. He believes what he’s saying. I don’t hold anything personally against him though he might find a ton of horse manure delivered to his house.
>
>  Just as a joke_.”

* * *

Looking back on this AI-scam is surreal in the light of 2026, where Zach now essentially exists, for real. I’m not entirely convinced today's LLMs are much more helpful than a 25-year-old furiously typing back responses. In my mind, it’s simply a different kind of con.

But I was curious what the players in the Zach story made of things now, nearly a decade on.

Support Webworm

Hi,

It can be a funny thing, writing an email newsletter. From the very beginning, it's been driven by things that I think are really important – stories that may not be told elsewhere; perspectives that don't get a lot of light. And because there are no advertisers here that I need to placate, there are no barriers to what I can publish.

In theory.

Because I admit that on a _few_ occasions, I've been worried that what I'm about to hit "send" on will cause readers to unsubscribe. That the subject matter will be too unpalatable, and that people will turn away. In the back of my head is the knowledge that without advertisers, I _need_ paying readers to keep this thing going.

Sometimes my "fears" are realised – this story about a youth group leader (a story I was proud of) caused a significant portion of my readers to cancel on me. I don't feel proud admitting I think this way sometimes, but it can play on my mind. So sometimes,_I_ become the barrier.

Today's newsletter is one of those. One of those that has me going, _"Uh oh"_. But I come back to that original reason: It's important. In addition to that, the person telling the story is braver than I could ever hope to be.

Lily Thomas (not her real name) wrote to me last year, after listening to the Webworm podcast episode about Barry Briskman:

> _“The Spaceman Barry story held a lot of shock and surprise with its twist ending, but, for me, this story is not new or surprising in any way. And while others might feel bewildered by Barry, I feel I understand him greatly. My Dad is a version of Barry."_

Over a period of around three months, Lily has been working with guest _Webworm_ writer Madeleine Holden to tell her story. While the subject matter is dark, it's also incredibly honest in a way we don't often get to see. And, yes, I also believe it's hopeful in a way.

For some, I hope this story is healing – in that it makes some readers feel seen and less alone. For others, I like to think this can be a conduit to some kind of understanding. I also believe stories like this are empathy machines, and I have an incredible amount of empathy and respect for Lily.

I also think Lily extends an amount of empathy in this story that could seem unfathomable to some. And each survivor is allowed to feel how they feel. But this is Lily's story, and it's my honor to be able to share it.

It goes without saying, but please read this story with care. It's illustrated with photos Lily took on a trip to Vancouver. _"A way of releasing some of my traumatic ties to the city, my childhood, and my dad."_

_David._

Jump To Comments

* * *

## The Monster & The Man

** _This is the story of Lily Thomas, an assistant professor living in California (not her real name). It was told in collaboration with Madeleine Holden, a writer based in New Zealand._**

I know, I know: I’d rather not think about it either. On the list of acceptable dinner-party topics, incest is somewhere between body fluids and genocide, and for good reason: we don’t want to face the unfaceable.

I never had a choice.

I want to tell you my story, and the story of my father, who sexually abused me. I won’t bombard you with gory details, but I have something to say about the complexity of being assaulted by direct kin. About the confusion and grey area it involves. About hating and not hating my father; the monster and the man. About the goodness and darkness in all of us.

* * *

My father was a bright guy. He lived paycheck to paycheck and was constantly in debt, but he was intensely analytical with an engineer’s brain, studying kinesiology at university and working on and off as a general contractor for construction projects. He was an eclectic reader and captivating storyteller. I’m sure I got my intellect from my dad—alongside my athleticism, curiosity and sense of wonder—and when I’m casting around for things to be grateful for, that’s something I find.

My father was a heavy and lifelong drinker. At age 10 he tried his first beer and that became his daily drink of choice, but when he occasionally turned to hard alcohol like Grand Marnier and Kahlua, it turned him into a darker person. On beer, he was obnoxious, telling theatrical stories and laughing loudly, but on hard alcohol he was like a cobra: the atmosphere would be still, calm and intense, and then he would strike. Sometimes he would literally strike my mum, other times he’d fake out with violent behavior and threats just to scare her.

His descent into alcoholism makes perfect sense: as a baby he lost his father in a gruesome boating accident and his mother and stepfather were heavy drinkers; the latter a cruel and violent man and the former beset by grief, schizophrenia and homelessness throughout her sad life. My dad didn’t have much of a start.

Still, he made a shot at normal family life when he married my mother at the age of 34. They had my brother, sister and me in quick succession, each 20 months apart, and their marriage unravelled soon after. Given the aforementioned drinking, violence and threats, she didn’t stick around for long. After they split, my mum remarried and had three kids with my stepdad, who also had two daughters from his previous marriage.

My full siblings and I would spend Mondays and every second weekend with our dad, with occasional one-on-one overnights. He didn’t remarry and struggled to pay child support. His houses were derelict and strange, with milk crates and fish tanks turned upside down and covered with a tablecloth or sheet to become nightstands, and sheets and towels hung over the curtains to help keep the cold out in winter.

Despite all this, my siblings idolised my father. I never could. As early as I can remember, my primary stance toward him was wariness. This was especially true when he was drunk.

Intoxicated, my father was strange. He’d make us watch age-inappropriate movies with him and lecture us with his life philosophies. If we weren't listening well enough, he'd pretend to have a heart attack and die, either erupting into laughter at his prank or laying motionless for a long time to see how we’d react. It was my role to corral my siblings into bed when he was in one of these moods.

And from the age of three until 12, my father would creep into my room late at night, drunk on spirits, and sexually assault me.

* * *

As a child, dissociation was my defence against these assaults, and I suppressed what happened to me. I went through my teens and early adulthood with the abuse sealed off from conscious awareness, meaning I didn’t view myself as a victim or survivor. (To this day, neither of those words sit right with me, for reasons I’ll get into soon.) Still, my body always held signs: a persistent pain in my legs, bed wetting till age 10, sexual difficulty in later years, and a bone-deep fear of the dark that lasted well into adulthood.

When I was 12, I moved with my mother, stepfather and siblings from Canada, where we grew up, to California. My father visited when he could, but contact with him felt like a strain, and our relationship began to deteriorate.

Still, at age 19, I went by myself to Canada to visit my dad, and stayed at his place. The house, which I hadn’t seen since I was 12, was exactly the same, down to the stuffed animals in my childhood room. Returning filled me with an icky feeling I couldn’t explain, and the first night I was there, I wet the bed. I was mortified: I was 19, this hadn’t happened to me in years, what was going on? But when I told my dad, he got this look on his face I’ll never forget: downcast eyes, looking sheepish and guilty, with a kind of knowingness I couldn’t place at the time. I never stayed with him again.

In my 20s, my relationship with my father deteriorated even further, and his alcoholism, money problems and mental health worsened. We remained in sporadic contact and I tried to help from afar, but I had a separate life in the United States while he was on a downward trajectory in Canada. In 2021, he died of liver cirrhosis.

It was only once I had this space from my father that I was able to face what he did to me through therapy, including EMDR, and the company of good friends with similar experiences. When I first came to terms with my experience, I cried tears of disbelief, grief, agony, confusion; screaming my lungs out with rage as I drove down the freeway. In one EMDR session, I imagined escaping my father’s abuse by running out of my childhood bedroom, throwing a lit match behind me and locking the door, leaving my father to burn.

Ultimately, though, it didn’t help to view my dad as pure evil. For a start, it didn’t feel true. What my father did to me was unforgiveable; yet he could also be kind and gentle. Sometimes he seemed seized by childhood innocence: before going to bed at night, for example, my dad would lead my siblings and me in the Now I Lay Me Down to Sleep prayer then have us all say, _"Something wonderful will happen to me tomorrow."_ He wanted us to believe good things were ahead of us; that the future was bright and anything could happen. I knew he was hoping this for himself too.

Defining people by the worst thing they’ve ever done doesn’t feel right to me. I hope I’m not remembered solely for the worst thing I’ve ever done. Sometimes people commit crimes so reprehensible that all their achievements and good qualities are overshadowed; I accept that. But it doesn’t mean their achievements or good qualities vanish.

I’ve come to see pure goodness and pure evil are fairytale ideas; a cop out in lieu of deeper thinking. Black/white, good/evil, are too easy. It's much harder to consider the middle, the grey, the complexity. I don’t think anyone is served by pretending people are wholly good or bad. Certainly not their victims.

That’s the other reason I reject the good/evil binary: it traps me in a mindset of fear. When I believe in evil people, my body shrinks in terror. When I believe in people who act out based on their own lived experiences, I don't have to be afraid. I can acknowledge that there will be people I don't want to engage with or be around based on their actions and choices – and I trust that I can handle myself, protect myself, around anyone who wants to cause me harm. They are not evil and I am not a victim.

I still sometimes hate my father. I do. I also pity him, feel grateful for him, wonder about him, puzzle over him. My feelings are complex and not fully resolved. My father died before I had a chance to confront him for what he did, and I wonder how I would react and relate to him if he were still alive. Would I confront him? Would he remember what he did to me, or was he too drunk? Would I cut off all contact? See what could be repaired between us? Forgive him if he apologised sincerely? I don't know how I would navigate any kind of relationship or interaction with him.

I want to stress that I’m not holding myself out as a spokesperson for survivors. I’m certainly not telling anyone how to feel about their own abuser.

But I’m not consoled by the image of my father as a two-dimensional monster. Ultimately, this is why I let it go: I find complexity more healing than caricatures; nuance more soothing than binaries. I can find space for all the realities of my father: his many faces, moods, modes and deeds; all the horror and the beauty. So I can find space for all of myself too.

 _-Lily, as told in collaboration with Madeleine Holden._

* * *

This piece has no paywall, and zero advertisements. Thanks to those of you who made this possible. If you think this piece could help anyone, you can share it using this link: www.webworm.co/lily

Hi,

It can be a funny thing, writing an email newsletter. From the very beginning, it's been driven by things that I think are really important – stories that may not be told elsewhere; perspectives that don't get a lot of light. And because there are no advertisers here that I need to placate, there are no barriers to what I can publish.

In theory.

Because I admit that on a _few_ occasions, I've been worried that what I'm about to hit "send" on will cause readers to unsubscribe. That the subject matter will be too unpalatable, and that people will turn away. In the back of my head is the knowledge that without advertisers, I _need_ paying readers to keep this thing going.

Sometimes my "fears" are realised – this story about a youth group leader (a story I was proud of) caused a significant portion of my readers to cancel on me. I don't feel proud admitting I think this way sometimes, but it can play on my mind. So sometimes,_I_ become the barrier.

Today's newsletter is one of those. One of those that has me going, _"Uh oh"_. But I come back to that original reason: It's important. In addition to that, the person telling the story is braver than I could ever hope to be.

Lily Thomas (not her real name) wrote to me last year, after listening to the Webworm podcast episode about Barry Briskman:

> _“The Spaceman Barry story held a lot of shock and surprise with its twist ending, but, for me, this story is not new or surprising in any way. And while others might feel bewildered by Barry, I feel I understand him greatly. My Dad is a version of Barry."_

Over a period of around three months, Lily has been working with guest _Webworm_ writer Madeleine Holden to tell her story. While the subject matter is dark, it's also incredibly honest in a way we don't often get to see. And, yes, I also believe it's hopeful in a way.

For some, I hope this story is healing – in that it makes some readers feel seen and less alone. For others, I like to think this can be a conduit to some kind of understanding. I also believe stories like this are empathy machines, and I have an incredible amount of empathy and respect for Lily.

I also think Lily extends an amount of empathy in this story that could seem unfathomable to some. And each survivor is allowed to feel how they feel. But this is Lily's story, and it's my honor to be able to share it.

It goes without saying, but please read this story with care. It's illustrated with photos Lily took on a trip to Vancouver. _"A way of releasing some of my traumatic ties to the city, my childhood, and my dad."_

_David._

Jump To Comments

## The Monster & The Man

** _This is the story of Lily Thomas, an assistant professor living in California (not her real name). It was told in collaboration with Madeleine Holden, a writer based in New Zealand._**

I know, I know: I’d rather not think about it either. On the list of acceptable dinner-party topics, incest is somewhere between body fluids and genocide, and for good reason: we don’t want to face the unfaceable.

I never had a choice.

I want to tell you my story, and the story of my father, who sexually abused me. I won’t bombard you with gory details, but I have something to say about the complexity of being assaulted by direct kin. About the confusion and grey area it involves. About hating and not hating my father; the monster and the man. About the goodness and darkness in all of us.

* * *

My father was a bright guy. He lived paycheck to paycheck and was constantly in debt, but he was intensely analytical with an engineer’s brain, studying kinesiology at university and working on and off as a general contractor for construction projects. He was an eclectic reader and captivating storyteller. I’m sure I got my intellect from my dad—alongside my athleticism, curiosity and sense of wonder—and when I’m casting around for things to be grateful for, that’s something I find.

My father was a heavy and lifelong drinker. At age 10 he tried his first beer and that became his daily drink of choice, but when he occasionally turned to hard alcohol like Grand Marnier and Kahlua, it turned him into a darker person. On beer, he was obnoxious, telling theatrical stories and laughing loudly, but on hard alcohol he was like a cobra: the atmosphere would be still, calm and intense, and then he would strike. Sometimes he would literally strike my mum, other times he’d fake out with violent behavior and threats just to scare her.

His descent into alcoholism makes perfect sense: as a baby he lost his father in a gruesome boating accident and his mother and stepfather were heavy drinkers; the latter a cruel and violent man and the former beset by grief, schizophrenia and homelessness throughout her sad life. My dad didn’t have much of a start.

Still, he made a shot at normal family life when he married my mother at the age of 34. They had my brother, sister and me in quick succession, each 20 months apart, and their marriage unravelled soon after. Given the aforementioned drinking, violence and threats, she didn’t stick around for long. After they split, my mum remarried and had three kids with my stepdad, who also had two daughters from his previous marriage.

My full siblings and I would spend Mondays and every second weekend with our dad, with occasional one-on-one overnights. He didn’t remarry and struggled to pay child support. His houses were derelict and strange, with milk crates and fish tanks turned upside down and covered with a tablecloth or sheet to become nightstands, and sheets and towels hung over the curtains to help keep the cold out in winter.

Despite all this, my siblings idolised my father. I never could. As early as I can remember, my primary stance toward him was wariness. This was especially true when he was drunk.

Intoxicated, my father was strange. He’d make us watch age-inappropriate movies with him and lecture us with his life philosophies. If we weren't listening well enough, he'd pretend to have a heart attack and die, either erupting into laughter at his prank or laying motionless for a long time to see how we’d react. It was my role to corral my siblings into bed when he was in one of these moods.

And from the age of three until 12, my father would creep into my room late at night, drunk on spirits, and sexually assault me.

* * *

As a child, dissociation was my defence against these assaults, and I suppressed what happened to me. I went through my teens and early adulthood with the abuse sealed off from conscious awareness, meaning I didn’t view myself as a victim or survivor. (To this day, neither of those words sit right with me, for reasons I’ll get into soon.) Still, my body always held signs: a persistent pain in my legs, bed wetting till age 10, sexual difficulty in later years, and a bone-deep fear of the dark that lasted well into adulthood.

When I was 12, I moved with my mother, stepfather and siblings from Canada, where we grew up, to California. My father visited when he could, but contact with him felt like a strain, and our relationship began to deteriorate.

Still, at age 19, I went by myself to Canada to visit my dad, and stayed at his place. The house, which I hadn’t seen since I was 12, was exactly the same, down to the stuffed animals in my childhood room. Returning filled me with an icky feeling I couldn’t explain, and the first night I was there, I wet the bed. I was mortified: I was 19, this hadn’t happened to me in years, what was going on? But when I told my dad, he got this look on his face I’ll never forget: downcast eyes, looking sheepish and guilty, with a kind of knowingness I couldn’t place at the time. I never stayed with him again.

In my 20s, my relationship with my father deteriorated even further, and his alcoholism, money problems and mental health worsened. We remained in sporadic contact and I tried to help from afar, but I had a separate life in the United States while he was on a downward trajectory in Canada. In 2021, he died of liver cirrhosis.

It was only once I had this space from my father that I was able to face what he did to me through therapy, including EMDR, and the company of good friends with similar experiences. When I first came to terms with my experience, I cried tears of disbelief, grief, agony, confusion; screaming my lungs out with rage as I drove down the freeway. In one EMDR session, I imagined escaping my father’s abuse by running out of my childhood bedroom, throwing a lit match behind me and locking the door, leaving my father to burn.

Ultimately, though, it didn’t help to view my dad as pure evil. For a start, it didn’t feel true. What my father did to me was unforgiveable; yet he could also be kind and gentle. Sometimes he seemed seized by childhood innocence: before going to bed at night, for example, my dad would lead my siblings and me in the Now I Lay Me Down to Sleep prayer then have us all say, _"Something wonderful will happen to me tomorrow."_ He wanted us to believe good things were ahead of us; that the future was bright and anything could happen. I knew he was hoping this for himself too.

Defining people by the worst thing they’ve ever done doesn’t feel right to me. I hope I’m not remembered solely for the worst thing I’ve ever done. Sometimes people commit crimes so reprehensible that all their achievements and good qualities are overshadowed; I accept that. But it doesn’t mean their achievements or good qualities vanish.

I’ve come to see pure goodness and pure evil are fairytale ideas; a cop out in lieu of deeper thinking. Black/white, good/evil, are too easy. It's much harder to consider the middle, the grey, the complexity. I don’t think anyone is served by pretending people are wholly good or bad. Certainly not their victims.

That’s the other reason I reject the good/evil binary: it traps me in a mindset of fear. When I believe in evil people, my body shrinks in terror. When I believe in people who act out based on their own lived experiences, I don't have to be afraid. I can acknowledge that there will be people I don't want to engage with or be around based on their actions and choices – and I trust that I can handle myself, protect myself, around anyone who wants to cause me harm. They are not evil and I am not a victim.

I still sometimes hate my father. I do. I also pity him, feel grateful for him, wonder about him, puzzle over him. My feelings are complex and not fully resolved. My father died before I had a chance to confront him for what he did, and I wonder how I would react and relate to him if he were still alive. Would I confront him? Would he remember what he did to me, or was he too drunk? Would I cut off all contact? See what could be repaired between us? Forgive him if he apologised sincerely? I don't know how I would navigate any kind of relationship or interaction with him.

I want to stress that I’m not holding myself out as a spokesperson for survivors. I’m certainly not telling anyone how to feel about their own abuser.

But I’m not consoled by the image of my father as a two-dimensional monster. Ultimately, this is why I let it go: I find complexity more healing than caricatures; nuance more soothing than binaries. I can find space for all the realities of my father: his many faces, moods, modes and deeds; all the horror and the beauty. So I can find space for all of myself too.

 _-Lily, as told in collaboration with Madeleine Holden._

external.description:
Hi,

There's a thing that happens in the news cycle that when a horrific story is over, the subject often drops off the radar – and we never hear from them again.

Jump To Comments

I didn't want that to be the case with Everlee Wihongi, the Kiwi kidnapped and imprisoned by ICE for 73 days.

So a few weeks ago, I made my way to Wisconsin to meet up with Everlee and her mother Betty, to check in. Throughout my reporting this year, I found Everlee to be incredibly strong, smart, and incredibly funny. Same thing with her mother.

In person, they were that – and then some.

I had so many questions: I wanted to know the details of the day she was released, and what it was like being dumped back into a life that had been put on hold for two and a half months. I had questions about Everlee's cellmates, and how she made it through.

With all that in mind, I've turned my day with Everlee into a 40 minute audio documentary, which you can listen to here:

* * *

Webworm Visits Everlee and Betty Wihongi

0:00

/2355.31932

1×

* * *

For those who prefer to read, I've also adapted that audio into a written piece below. If you can listen, do: In reading, you perhaps miss some of the nuance of how Everlee and Betty phrase things. But I wanted it to be as accessible as possible.

* * *

## A Quick Note On Webworm

All my public interest journalism, like this piece, is powered by my paying readers. They let me purchase a flight to Wisconsin, hire a car, pay for petrol, and pay my audio editor in New Zealand.

To clarify how _Webworm_ works, I wanted to share an email I got from a reader, and my reply. They were a bit annoyed that my last article _(in which I released_ all my funding information_)_ was behind a paywall:


> **To: davidfarrier@protonmail.com
>  From: V
> Date: August 2**
>
> David, something I do not like is how you provide all your followers, paying and non-paying, with a taunting morsel of a story then you shut the door and will re-open it for the final chapter only if the follower pays. I am a pensioner so am not in a position to always pay for the closing chapters of your stories.
>
> In fact, so disenchanted am I with capitalism that I am a strong advocate of a Resource Based Economy… renowned American social engineer, Jacque Fresco, conceived of this brilliant moneyless system where, with the advent of AI, there will no longer be the need for money. You may wish to read all about him and his great vision. He came to New Zealand some years ago and laid out his vision in a presentation. The brilliance of this genius was inspiring... any question put to him during the Q & A section was satisfied and silenced with utter wisdom.
>
> So, as you may have guessed by now, I consider information should be a free commodity available to humanity at large… charging for it is, in my respectful view, petty.

I replied with this:

> Thanks for writing, and reading my stuff.
>
> Generally, I'd say about 60% of my stuff (all my public interest journalism: My Everlee coverage, ICE, megachurches, bad people doing bad things etc) goes out for free, with zero ads (Webworm will never run ads).
>
> Sometimes, I will send examples of paywalled stuff to those in the free list, which is I think what has got your goat here.
>
> I get it, but to be frank: I need people to realise there is more in the paid Webworm, and my hope is that people will hopefully come on board - and I can continue to afford to pay writers and lawyers, be able to travel to cover stories on the ground etc, and keep doing my thing.
>
> In the FAQ (webworm.co/about) - and I have said this many times in free newsletters over the years - I have a 50% off deal, but am happy to comp people if they can't afford it: those on a sickness benefit, students, beneficiaries etc.
>
> Which I have just done for you. I never want anyone stretched beyond their means, ever.
>
> Anyway, if you login at www.webworm.co with your email, you will be able to access everything. And make any updates to your account, too - change email addresses, turn Webworm emails on and off etc.
>
> I hope this explains things a little.

 __I'm going to be in__ _****Toronto****_ __next week, and will do doing a Webworm meetup for subscribers. If you're interested in attending, email me: davidfarrier@protonmail.com.__

## **Webworm Visits Wisconsin**

** _by David Farrier_**

Getting to see Everlee in person involved a three hour flight from Los Angeles to Dallas, then another two hours from Dallas to Madison. Then it’s a two hour drive northeast, up to a small town where her mum lives, which is where Everlee Wihongi is currently staying.

I drive past cornfield after cornfield – _there’s a lot of corn in this part of Wisconsin –_ before pulling into a little subdivision, a typical little American slice of life.

I park up, and an incredibly mellow black and white dog comes out to greet me, tail wagging. Everlee's dog, Dartangan.

It’s kind of strange, meeting this person I know so much about, but have never actually seen in person. The first thing that strikes me about Everlee is that she looks so happy: Dressed in a black tee, she’s beaming.

She passes on apologies from her dad, who just went to work. As I’d been travelling, they’d all been celebrating her nephew’s 1st birthday with the family._“A huge one-year-old, massive, typical Polynesian baby,”_ she laughs.

I’m mainly struck by how normal everything seems – talking about kids and dogs.

But her year has been anything but normal. Over 70 days locked up in various ICE prisons, before being suddenly spat back out into the life she was living before. Well, _sort of_ the life she was living before.

A lot can change in three months.

__Dartangan, happy for a visitor.__

The day I visit, Everlee’s been free for about six weeks. I ask her to take me through the day she got released from prison.

> They woke me up at 1.30 in the morning. The guard comes and she knocks, and unlocked my door and she goes, “You're leaving”. And so I immediately shot out of the bed and I rolled up my sheets, got all packed up. I had written notes already because I knew I'd be getting out soon. And so I was running through the hallways, sliding them under people's doors. The guard came back, and I was sitting downstairs, and she goes, “What are you doing out?” And I go, “You said I was leaving!” And she goes, “You're not leaving till 3.30!” And I look at the clock and it's only 1.30.
>
> And so I just had to sit there and tool around. They made me sit in my room. I'd given heaps of my stuff away. But at 3.30, they opened the doors to let me out, and we went down to this place called South intake. When we got in there, they took all of our things. There were two guards there: A girl and a boy. And they [had] pretty short fuses. And so when we go in there they're yelling at us, “Put your stuff down, go get changed!”
>
> The guards were quite horrible to us. I had my backpack that got brought in from the airport, plus I had all the property I had accumulated: Books, papers, notebooks and stuff. So I had two boxes there, and he goes, “You're going to have to fit everything into this paper bag”. And then I started getting angry and I started swearing at him. I just said, “I didn't pick to come here from the airport. This is all my stuff, I'm not leaving anything here!”

I could understand why she was frustrated. Think of the one carry-on bag you take on a plane: It’s full of your most important things. There’s a reason you didn’t check it in.

Then all the stuff from her life for the last 73 days: Letters from prison mates, stories she had scrawled down, memories she needed to process once she was out. You can’t just let go of that.

Standing up for herself worked out: She got to keep her things – not just a paper bag’s worth.

Then she turned her attention to others in the room.

> There was this lady that had cancer, who had been waiting to be transported. She was dressed in orange. And every time [the guards] would go out, the door would slam. And they kept doing it to her, and just looking past her, and so I said, “Stop slamming the door on that sick lady's face.”
>
> And she says, “I didn't see her.” I was like, “You didn't see her in the bright orange with the walker, in front of the white wall? That's probably really horrible for her.”

By now it was 12.30pm, and all the prisoners began to be placed in shackles and loaded onto the bus. She was used to being moved around by this point – court dates missed because ICE would just randomly shunt her to another facility.

But right from the start, this trip felt more hopeful.

> There was the bus driver. He was so cool. He was talking in Spanish. I was just standing there and I go, “Oh my God, I don't speak Spanish. I'm sorry.” And he goes, “You’re the only person in this whole facility that doesn't speak Spanish!” But then he goes, “Where are you from?” And I go, “New Zealand.” He goes, “Oh, you're a Māori. That's so cool. You're the first one I've ever met!” – and he came and shook my hand.
>
> They’re putting on the belly belt and the shackles, and I'm just grumbling: “I don't want to wear the leg shackles. I hate wearing them.” And [the bus driver] just looks and he goes, “Dang, it looks like you need big boy ones for your big boy ankles! And I don't have any!” And I go, “Must be I don't need them then.” And he goes, “I don't have any, so you can't wear them!”
>
> So I didn't have to have my legs shackled. He was so cool.

 __The Eloy Detention Centre.__

The bus set off from the Eloy Detention Centre, briefly stopping at another ICE facility in Florence – a place known for charming things like regular measles outbreaks. Then it was a few hours north to the city of Phoenix. She tells me most people on the bus were sleeping, after what had been a very long night.

They were woken up again as the bus pulled into a Department of Homeland Security facility.

> That's when people panicked and they thought that we were just getting dropped off there and transported to a different facility. But the bus driver said, “No, everybody can relax. You're all going home today.”

Imagine hearing those words:  _You're all going home today._

From there, it was the final leg to the Visitor Centre. I ask – after all the ups and downs of the last three months, coming close to freedom so many times before being thwarted – when she knew this was actually it. That her ordeal was over.

> It was when we were actually getting off the bus. And everybody in the bus was like, “I can't believe it.” And then we're all hugging each other, even hugging the guards.

A local church group was there waiting with boxes of food, drinks and clothing. This wasn’t some state funded group or official part of the ICE process – they were just volunteers, mutual aid at its finest.

> I called my mum right away, she was the first one. And then I called the family group chat. They thought that my grandmother was calling everybody by accident again! And so they all kind of slowly hopped on there. I was just, “Hi.”
>
> Then we have a cousins’ group chat from our holiday. I saw my aunt posted your [Webworm] thing. “Everlee has been released.” And so they had put that in the group chat. And so then the cousins started trying to call, and it was wicked. It was really cool.

She made her way from the visitors centre in Phoenix, to an Airbnb her parents had booked. She couldn’t check into a hotel, because she’d discovered ICE had kept her passport and ID.

> When I got to the Airbnb, my cousin called because she was like, “Are you alright?” And I go, “Ah, a bit weird being alone, eh?” And so she talked to me for hours. Then she called her sister, and so it was probably six of us FaceTiming all at the same time, just till my parents got there.

It had been 73 days since Everlee had last seen her mum and dad.

* * *

At this point, I hear a car pull in. Betty is back from work. It’s the first time I’ve met her mum in person, too – and she’s got a grin as big as her daughters. She hands me two bottles of "Sun Drop" – a drink she swears by – before telling me what Everlee's release day was like for her.

> We had rented an Airbnb for Everlee to wait at, because she didn't have any ID – so she couldn't go in a hotel. And Gordon and I scrambled and we found an AirBnB and we got it, gave her the address, she got an Uber there. And then I just said, “Wait there and go shower, swim. Wait for us. We'll be there later on, and your brothers will be there too."
>
> So we walk in and she's there. Her two brothers and my daughter-in-law were there waiting. I went to hug Everlee and one of them had picked up her phone and I just looked at them like, “No!”

There were a lot of hugs, and I understand the temptation to take some photos.

> I think I just kind of gave them the look like: “No photos right now.” Yeah. "Someone will die tonight if that happens!"

Everlee chips in.

> My dad's not a hugger. Before this, he had given me two hugs in my whole life. And he gave me one right when he got there - and then when it was going, he gave me another hug. And I'm like, “Dad, you've doubled the amount of hugs I've ever gotten in my life!” He's like, “Ah, get lost!”

She says that first night out, while amazing, was also incredibly difficult.

> It was so weird. There was a huge bed. I had a king-size bed, but I stayed in [the corner] like the same size as the cot. I didn't expand from there. It wasn't a good sleep. I kept hearing the keychains, you know, keychains jingling – so I would just open my eyes and then realize I wasn't in there. And then when I would fall asleep, I'd hear, “Cuenta!” and so I'd just go to stand up.
>
> “Cuenta” is count, but as most people spoke Spanish, that's what they'd say. They'd just say “cuenta”, and then you'd have to stand up by your door. And then they would walk past the door, you know, look at the slip, make sure it matched up with your badge and your face, and then you could go back to bed. And so the first couple of days, I just kept hearing that and the keychains.
>
> I have these little bouts when I'm by myself. Just bouts of despair. The therapist said it's like survivor's guilt. I feel happy that I'm out, but I feel sad for my mates that I just stuck in there like Lucy. She's stuck in there indefinitely and she had been there for 12 months, so she's been there for 14 months now. And she's not going to get to see an immigration judge.

Lucy was from Bulgaria, and was one of her best mates inside. She feels like she’s left her friend behind. She can’t stop thinking about her.

> Her husband died two months before she got taken by ICE. They were superintendents of an apartment complex, and so her address was there because she was taking care of it. Her husband died, so there was nobody to look after the apartment. She has no address, she has no documents. She's got no family to help her at all, no way to see a judge, no lawyer, nothing. No help. I don't know what's going to happen to her.

There are others, too. She got some of them to write their stories down – Everlee has them in a notebook. Again, that’s why she fought so hard to keep all her stuff. She carries all these stories with her, on repeat, in her brain.

> Just innocent people. [Another] girl in the wrong place at the wrong time: She came from Nicaragua, and she's been stuck for nine months now. No way out. And she's not a criminal, she was a medical assistant.

Mainly, Everlee realises that as bad as she had it, she had a family in the US battling for her every day. So many of her new friends didn’t have that. And so they remain in prison, no end in sight.

And Everlee, well, she’s just landed back in the life she had before. She emerged as a different person. And she’s emerged into different circumstances.

> My job let me go because I was stuck in there. You know, well, I don't want to say bad things about them. They looked after my job for a bit.

She’d had a really good job as a welder – that’s gone now. She doesn’t want to sleep alone, so she’d moved back to her parents place while she tries to readjust.

In all of this, she’s still so upbeat. I have no doubt she’s putting on a brave face for me – a stranger in her house – but I have no doubt her glass half full approach has helped her through this.

> I still have a place. And that money from the GoFundMe helped me keep that. And I have the most supportive friends in the world. They know that I was overwhelmed when I came out. And so they didn't jump on me. They just messaged, “When you're ready, we're here to talk, but you know I'm glad you're out.”
>
> Two weeks ago, my best friend planned a seafood boil, and invited a bunch of our friends, and oh, it was so nice. They were so happy to see me. Everybody that was invited came. The food was really good. She knew I loved seafood, and so she went around different places to find the best seafood. Not just anything, the best.

* * *

I ask her how she kept her shit together inside. The different facilities, the transport, having court dates thwarted, the lack of control over her own life.

> So there were... moments.
>
> I didn't cry in front of anybody. I would, you know, I'd go take a shower, that would be where I would have little breakdowns. But I didn't want people to see me crying. I just wanted to keep it together too, just keep myself calm.
>
> I feel like I learned, I practiced a lot of self-control in there. I tried to stay calm all the time. It was hard some days. If I knew that if I was having a bad day, I would just message on the tablet. I'd message [my family] and just say, “Look, can you please let everybody know I'm not going to be calling today. I don't feel like going down on the phones, and I'm having a bad day. I just want to stay in my bed.”

She says the main trick she found was just trying to make this very un-normal time feel normal. Little tricks that made her feel like she’d never been kidnapped by ICE in the first place.

> I was having the worst time at Adelanto. It took me a couple of days there, but then when I realized we can go outside at 7.30am, I'm just going to get up early. I'm going to get out early, I'm gonna work-out, outside.
>
> I started making myself a little routine. Like I did things to make myself feel normal. I love wearing makeup. So I made eyeliner there. I'd put it on every day. I'd have a shower, do my hair. And then I learned how to make these fancy ‘Starbucks’ coffees. I had a peanut butter jar. And so I was making really fancy coffee drinks for myself, little iced coffees, and I'd go outside with them too. And people are like, “Where'd you get that?” I'm like, “I made it.” I put little designs on my coffee. So I did things to make myself feel normal, as normal as I could.
>
> But you just felt helpless often too, you know? The transport - I'd never felt so helpless before in my life. Because it was just being herded around. With the shackles, you're going where they tell you to go. And when you need to go to the bathroom, you just get one hand out of your shackles. It was the way that you were treated like farm animals: You'd try and ask questions, and they'd wave you off. I'm very particular about things, too. And so that was one of the hardest things for me was just not being able to really even advocate for myself, or advocate for others around. You just had to do what they wanted, when they wanted you to do it.
>
> It's a humiliating experience. I think [back] to when we were transported: Like, people were crying on the plane. Lots of people. They didn't know what was happening. They were taking people from California and moving them further away from their families, people that would visit them. Things like that.

Now, she has to figure out how to live her life, with all of that still in her head.

> I mean, it's left a very dirty mark on America for me. I'm so proud to be from New Zealand and I love going back there, and I love telling people I'm from New Zealand. I feel like, just the way I was treated, and the way they treated people that I've seen – I just feel like that's not part of the American dream. That's not part of the America I want to be in.

So while she’s happy to be back with her family, her friends and her dog, she also moves through the world now with a certain amount of worry. A certain amount of dread.

> It's hard after something like this. I just feel I pay taxes here, I contribute to my community here, I did a lot. And just the way that I was treated was just so mind boggling. I still can't really believe it.
>
> I think being out, I do feel anxious. I feel very anxious. You know, if I got pulled over by the police and ICE were to come, like, what would they find? I feel like anything, any excuse to fill a bed in one of the detention centers, to make the place a bit more money. I don't think anybody's really safe from them.
>
> For all the people that I met that are stuck in there, like immigrants, innocent people. And the people that I saw weren't the criminals that Donald Trump said. They were housewives, business owners.
>
> I keep going back to the transport, but they gave us all our regular clothes when we left. And there were people that were in their high-vis, they still had mud on their pants. There was a pregnant lady, there were children. It was just these people that they picked up on the job sites! that's not a criminal person, you picked them up from work, you know?

I ask Betty how she’s holding up.

> I’m just relieved. I didn't really realize how affected I was. I thought I was doing pretty good at keeping things together, and after Everlee came home I was at work, and my boss came in and he's like, “I'm really glad Everlee’s back”, and I said, “Yeah, me too.”
>
> And he goes, “It's just nice to have you back.” I'm like, “What?” He goes, “You've been really dark. You've really dark, and we didn’t know what to do.”

I think back to how when all this started, New Zealand’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Winston Peters, went on the TV news and confirmed to a nation why the New Zealander had been detained at LAX.

__Winston Peters, talking about Everlee on New Zealand's 6pm news bulletins.__

His confirmation was false, we know that now. He said she’d failed to fill in some forms. Like she’d been hiding something. That she got what she deserved.

A narrative that a lot of people in New Zealand still believe. Look at the comments section under various news stories on social media and Winston’s narrative stuck: _She wasn’t to be trusted. She brought all this upon herself._

Betty pauses.

> I'm just... you know, looking back now, Winston Peters, he... he worries me for our country, he really does. He's like a mini-Trump in New Zealand for me. But just someone who can brazenly lie and tell people, “Oh, Everlee didn't fill out some forms correctly, she missed information.”
>
> Just to blatantly lie like that was just, I couldn't believe it.
>
> And then at first I thought, maybe he didn't know. And I'm like, “But he's the Minister of Foreign Affairs. How can he not know?” And then you come to the realisation that he just straight out lied. He's a liar. A bald-faced liar.

She had some kind things to say about the New Zealand consulate, after they finally got onboard. She also spoke favourably of Labour’s Phil Twyford, and the Maori party.

I ask if Betty plans to stay in the US herself. And, as expected, the answer isn’t straightforward.

> It's a very scary time. You know, I worry for Everlee, of this happening to her again. I worry about [my other children]. You know, we've got two people that aren't citizens and it's very worrisome. And the new things that they're coming up with, like the Naturalization Bill that they tried to push through. It failed once, but it doesn't mean that they are not going to push it, try again. So it's worrisome.
>
> We had planned on leaving when [my husband] Gordon retired, and he's looking at retiring this year. But then our kids went and had kids, kids who love us and want to be around us, and call us, and that's made it difficult for us to want to leave.

* * *

There’s been a lot of beeping while we talk, Everlee getting up and down to the kitchen. She says she saw a viral recipe for artichokes online, and she’s been making them while we talk.

We ended up eating too many of those viral artichokes, to the point that when we went out to dinner later that night we couldn’t even begin to finish what we’d ordered.

I drove back off into the corn, driving back to Madison. Betty texts me to make sure I made it back safely.

I had.

The next day, some messages from Everlee, too. She's sent me a video. It’s eight seconds long, and is soundtracked by music blasting from a speaker.

It’s a terrifically bright day, and she’s out in the middle of a lake on a paddle board, surrounded by sparking blue water and a giant sky.

It’s just her.

And while she has a long road to recovery in front of her, right now she feels about as free as any human could be.

 __Everlee's view from her paddle board.__

Everlee still has a GoFundMe that anyone is welcome to contribute to, as she looks for work and gets her life back on track.

Hi,

There's a thing that happens in the news cycle that when a horrific story is over, the subject often drops off the radar – and we never hear from them again.

Jump To Comments

I didn't want that to be the case with Everlee Wihongi, the Kiwi kidnapped and imprisoned by ICE for 73 days.

So a few weeks ago, I made my way to Wisconsin to meet up with Everlee and her mother Betty, to check in. Throughout my reporting this year, I found Everlee to be incredibly strong, smart, and incredibly funny. Same thing with her mother.

In person, they were that – and then some.

I had so many questions: I wanted to know the details of the day she was released, and what it was like being dumped back into a life that had been put on hold for two and a half months. I had questions about Everlee's cellmates, and how she made it through.

With all that in mind, I've turned my day with Everlee into a 40 minute audio documentary, which you can listen to here:

Webworm Visits Everlee and Betty Wihongi
0:00
/2355.31932

For those who prefer to read, I've also adapted that audio into a written piece below. If you can listen, do: In reading, you perhaps miss some of the nuance of how Everlee and Betty phrase things. But I wanted it to be as accessible as possible.

A Quick Note On Webworm

All my public interest journalism, like this piece, is powered by my paying readers. They let me purchase a flight to Wisconsin, hire a car, pay for petrol, and pay my audio editor in New Zealand.

To clarify how Webworm works, I wanted to share an email I got from a reader, and my reply. They were a bit annoyed that my last article (in which I released all my funding information) was behind a paywall:

To: davidfarrier@protonmail.com
From: V
Date: August 2

David, something I do not like is how you provide all your followers, paying and non-paying, with a taunting morsel of a story then you shut the door and will re-open it for the final chapter only if the follower pays. I am a pensioner so am not in a position to always pay for the closing chapters of your stories.

In fact, so disenchanted am I with capitalism that I am a strong advocate of a Resource Based Economy… renowned American social engineer, Jacque Fresco, conceived of this brilliant moneyless system where, with the advent of AI, there will no longer be the need for money. You may wish to read all about him and his great vision. He came to New Zealand some years ago and laid out his vision in a presentation. The brilliance of this genius was inspiring... any question put to him during the Q & A section was satisfied and silenced with utter wisdom.

So, as you may have guessed by now, I consider information should be a free commodity available to humanity at large… charging for it is, in my respectful view, petty.

I replied with this:

Thanks for writing, and reading my stuff.

Generally, I'd say about 60% of my stuff (all my public interest journalism: My Everlee coverage, ICE, megachurches, bad people doing bad things etc) goes out for free, with zero ads (Webworm will never run ads).

Sometimes, I will send examples of paywalled stuff to those in the free list, which is I think what has got your goat here.

I get it, but to be frank: I need people to realise there is more in the paid Webworm, and my hope is that people will hopefully come on board - and I can continue to afford to pay writers and lawyers, be able to travel to cover stories on the ground etc, and keep doing my thing.

In the FAQ (webworm.co/about) - and I have said this many times in free newsletters over the years - I have a 50% off deal, but am happy to comp people if they can't afford it: those on a sickness benefit, students, beneficiaries etc.

Which I have just done for you. I never want anyone stretched beyond their means, ever.

Anyway, if you login at www.webworm.co with your email, you will be able to access everything. And make any updates to your account, too - change email addresses, turn Webworm emails on and off etc.

I hope this explains things a little.
Upcoming Webworm Events

I'm going to be in Toronto next week, and will do doing a Webworm meetup for subscribers. If you're interested in attending, email me: davidfarrier@protonmail.com.
